chapters.title: Forgive and Forgiveness
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, forgiveness is a release: a burden lifted, a debt cancelled, a slate wiped clean
chapters.nutshell: The Bible has no single word for “forgive”. Hebrew uses a cluster of vivid pictures: God pardons, lifts and carries sin away, covers it, wipes it out and passes over it. Greek adds the ideas of releasing a captive and cancelling a debt as a free gift. Read through Jewish eyes, forgiveness is not a legal trick that leaves the debt in place; it is a real release that sets people free and restores relationships, with God and with one another.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical forgiveness means God (and we) really let go of what is owed, setting the other person free and restoring the relationship.
skeleton: We often think of forgiveness as a feeling or a legal verdict
Hebrew offers many pictures: pardon, lift, cover, wipe out, pass over
Only God is the subject of salach: true pardon belongs to him
Greek aphesis means release, and echoes the Jubilee year of liberty
In Jesus' Aramaic world, sin is a debt, and forgiving is cancelling it
Jewish tradition joins God's forgiveness to repentance and to making things right with people
Jesus forgives with God's authority and asks us to forgive freely

sections.h: What we usually assume
p: When most of us hear the word **forgive**, we think of one of two things. Either it is a feeling, letting go of anger inside, or it is a legal verdict, where a judge declares a guilty person “not guilty” while the debt is quietly paid by someone else behind the scenes.

The Bible is richer than both. It has no single word for forgiveness. Instead the Hebrew Scriptures use a whole family of word-pictures, and the Greek New Testament adds a few more. Each one shows a different side of the same gift. Looking at them one by one helps us see what God actually does when he forgives, and what he asks us to do for others.

sections.h: Salach: the pardon only God gives
p: The most direct Hebrew word is *salach* (to pardon) and its noun *selichah* (pardon, forgiveness). Something striking stands out: in the Hebrew Bible, **only God is ever the subject of salach**. People ask for it, but God alone gives it.

When Israel rebelled in the wilderness, Moses prayed, “Pardon the iniquity of this people,” and God answered, “I have pardoned, according to your word” (Numbers 14:19–20). The psalmist sings, “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). Notice the surprising logic: forgiveness does not make people careless about God; it draws them to him in awe and love.

From this word comes *Selichot*, the penitential prayers Jews recite in the days before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and a central blessing of the daily Amidah prayer: “Forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned… Blessed are You, LORD, who is gracious and forgives abundantly.”

sections.h: Lifting, covering, wiping, passing over
p: The other Hebrew words are pictures taken from everyday life. *Nasa* means to **lift up and carry**. When God reveals his name to Moses, he is the one “forgiving (lifting) iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:7). Sin is pictured as a heavy load, and God picks it up and carries it away. Micah asks, “Who is a God like you, lifting iniquity and passing over transgression?” (Micah 7:18).

*Kasah* means to **cover**: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is lifted, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1; see also 85:2). *Kipper*, the Temple word for atonement, means to cover or, more exactly, to purge and cleanse: “On this day atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you” (Leviticus 16:30).

*Machah* means to **wipe out or blot out**, like wiping a writing tablet clean. David begs, “Blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1, 9), and God promises, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25). Finally *avar* means to **pass over**, to walk on by without holding the offence against someone (Micah 7:18).

sections.h: Aphesis: release and Jubilee
p: The main New Testament verb is *aphiēmi*, and its noun *aphesis*. The basic meaning is **to let go, release, send away**. The same verb is used for leaving nets, releasing a prisoner, or cancelling a debt. The disciples “left (*aphentes*) their nets” to follow Jesus (Mark 1:18). Forgiveness, then, is not first a feeling; it is **letting something go**.

This word carries a strong Jewish echo. In the Septuagint, the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, *aphesis* translates the “release” of the Sabbath year and the “liberty” of the Jubilee, when debts were cancelled, slaves were freed and land returned to its families (Leviticus 25:10; Deuteronomy 15:1–2). When Jesus opens his ministry in Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61:1: he has come “to proclaim **liberty** (*aphesis*) to the captives… to set at **liberty** those who are oppressed” (Luke 4:18).
> In Jesus' world, forgiveness and Jubilee are the same word. To be forgiven is to be released: the debt cancelled, the prisoner set free, the inheritance given back.

sections.h: Forgiveness as a gift, a release and a passing over
p: Other Greek words fill out the picture. *Charizomai* comes from *charis*, grace, and means **to give freely, to forgive as a gift**. In Jesus' story of two debtors, the lender “graciously forgave them both” (Luke 7:42–43). Paul uses it when he says, “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32), and “having forgiven us all our trespasses” (Colossians 2:13).

*Apolyō* means **to release or set loose**: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And *paresis*, used only once, means **passing over**: God in his patience “passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25). This echoes the Hebrew *avar* of Micah 7:18. Every one of these words describes God truly letting go, not simply collecting payment from another source.

sections.h: Sin as a debt: “forgive us our debts”
p: Jesus taught in a world where people spoke Aramaic. In Aramaic the word *ḥova* means both **“debt” and “sin”**. That is why Matthew's version of the Lord's Prayer says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), while Luke's version says “sins” and then “everyone who is indebted to us” (Luke 11:4). The two ideas are one.

This shapes how we understand forgiveness. When a lender forgives a debt, nobody pays it; the lender **absorbs the loss** out of generosity. That is the point of Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant, whose huge debt the king simply cancelled (Matthew 18:23–35). A debt that is forgiven is not a debt that is paid. The servant's failure was not a legal error but a failure to let the mercy he received flow on to others.

sections.h: The Jewish context: teshuvah and Yom Kippur
p: In Jewish thought, forgiveness goes hand in hand with *teshuvah*, “returning” or repentance: turning back to God and to his ways. Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the great annual day of cleansing and forgiveness (Leviticus 16:30). Yet the Mishnah adds a famous rule: “For sins between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones. For sins between a person and their neighbour, the Day of Atonement does not atone until they have made peace with their neighbour” (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

Jesus says the same thing: “If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there… First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24). Later Hebrew even has a separate word for the forgiveness people give each other: *mechilah*, “letting go” of a claim, as when a lender waives a debt. Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally ask family and friends for *mechilah*.

sections.h: Jesus and the apostles
p: Because *salach* belonged to God alone, the scribes were shocked when Jesus told a paralysed man, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” They asked, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:5–7). Their question was exactly right from the Hebrew Bible, and that is the point: Jesus was acting with God's own authority, and he proved it by healing the man (Mark 2:10–12).

On the cross Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The apostles then proclaimed “forgiveness (*aphesis*) of sins” in his name (Acts 2:38; 10:43). Forgiveness was not only a private transaction; it formed a new community of released people who were to release one another (Colossians 3:13).

sections.h: Living it out
p: Common Western thinking can make forgiveness either a private feeling or a courtroom ruling where someone else is punished in our place. The Jewish lens shows something warmer and more practical: **God really lets go**, and he invites us to do the same. Forgiveness is a release that restores relationships.

This also means forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened. The person who did wrong is called to *teshuvah*: to turn, to apologise and, where possible, to make things right. The person who was wronged is called to release the debt, as God released ours. Ask yourself today: whose debt am I still holding? And is there someone whose forgiveness I need to ask for before I bring my worship to God?

chapters.title: Punishment and Discipline
chapters.subtitle: When God corrects, the Bible's words point to a parent training a child and a refiner purifying silver
chapters.trueMeaning: Correction, training and refining that restores
chapters.nutshell: We tend to hear “punishment” as pain paid back for wrongdoing. The Hebrew and Greek words behind it are more varied: God “visits” and attends to wrongs, sin carries its own consequences, discipline is a parent's training, and fire refines silver rather than destroying it. Greek writers even distinguished correction for the sufferer's good from revenge for the punisher's satisfaction. Read through a Jewish lens, God's judgments aim to set things right and to bring people home.
chapters.bigIdea: In the Bible, God's discipline is mainly the loving correction of a parent and refiner, aimed at healing and setting things right.
skeleton: We usually picture punishment as pain paid back
Paqad: God “visits”, attending to wrongs and to people in need
Avon: sin and its consequence are one word
Yasar and musar: discipline is training, like a parent with a child
Tsaraph and shaphat: refining fire and judging that rescues the weak
Greek kolasis, timōria, paideia, dikē and ekdikēsis each add a shade
God's correction comes from love and aims at restoration

sections.h: What we usually assume
p: For many people the word **punishment** means one thing: pain paid back to someone who did wrong, so that justice is “balanced”. If we picture God that way, he can seem like a strict judge who mainly wants each sin repaid.

The Bible's words are wider and warmer. Hebrew and Greek have several different terms that our English Bibles often flatten into “punish”. Some describe a parent training a child. Some describe a metal-worker refining silver. Some describe a judge rescuing the oppressed. Looking at them carefully does not make sin less serious; it shows **why** God deals with it and **what he is aiming at**.

sections.h: Paqad and avon: God attends to wrongs
p: The Hebrew verb *paqad* basically means **to visit, attend to, take note of**. When God “visited” Sarah, he gave her the son he had promised (Genesis 21:1). Joseph told his brothers, “God will surely visit you” and bring you out of Egypt (Genesis 50:24). The same verb is used when God “visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children” (Exodus 20:5; 34:7). God is not indifferent: he attends to wrongs as well as to needs.

Exodus 34:6–7 also sets this in proportion: God is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger,” keeping steadfast love “for thousands”, while the consequences of sin reach “the third and fourth generation”, which many explain as the members of one living household. Mercy is far larger than judgment.

*Avon* means **iniquity**, but it can also mean the **consequence** that grows out of iniquity. When Cain says, “My punishment is greater than I can bear” (Genesis 4:13), the word is *avon*. Hebrew sees sin and its results as one thing: wrongdoing carries its own harm within it, like a seed that grows into its own fruit.

sections.h: Yasar and musar: discipline as training
p: The verb *yasar* and its noun *musar* mean **discipline, instruction, training**. The book of Proverbs opens by saying it was written “to know wisdom and instruction (*musar*)” (Proverbs 1:2). The same word is used for teaching and for correction, because in Hebrew thinking they belong together.

“My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline (*musar*) or be weary of his reproof (*tochachat*), for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11–12). Moses says, “As a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you” (Deuteronomy 8:5). *Tochachat* means **correction or rebuke**: showing someone clearly where they went wrong so they can change.
> The picture is not a courtroom but a family. The one who disciplines is a father who delights in his child, and the goal is a wise, mature son or daughter.

sections.h: Tsaraph and shaphat: refining and setting right
p: *Tsaraph* means **to refine or smelt**, the way a metal-worker melts silver to remove the waste. God says of his people, “I will put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver… They will call upon my name, and I will answer them” (Zechariah 13:9). Malachi pictures the Lord sitting “as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3). Refining fire is painful, but its aim is to **keep the silver and lose the dross**.

*Shaphat* means **to judge**, but in Hebrew judging is mostly about setting things right. “Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute” (Psalm 82:3). A biblical judge was a rescuer, which is why the leaders in the book of Judges were deliverers. When the psalms cry out for God to judge, they are often begging him to come and save.

sections.h: Kolasis and timōria: correction or revenge?
p: In Greek, *kolasis* is the usual word for punishment. Its verb, *kolazō*, first meant to **cut back, prune or check** a plant's growth, and came to mean to correct or punish. *Timōria*, by contrast, meant **retribution**: a penalty that pays back and vindicates the honour of the one who was wronged.

The philosopher Aristotle drew a clear line between them: *kolasis* is inflicted for the sake of the one who suffers it, while *timōria* is for the sake of the one who inflicts it, to satisfy him (Rhetoric 1.10). In the New Testament, *kolasis* appears in Matthew 25:46 (“eternal punishment”) and 1 John 4:18 (“fear has to do with punishment”). *Timōria* appears only once, in Hebrews 10:29 (“how much worse punishment”).

Scholars **debate** how much Aristotle's distinction still applied in the first century; ordinary Greek did not always keep the two words apart. So we should not build a whole doctrine on one word. But it is worth knowing that the word Matthew uses to report Jesus' saying in 25:46 was, in its basic sense, a word for correction.

sections.h: Paideia, dikē, ekdikēsis and basanos
p: *Paideia* comes from *pais*, child, and means **child-training, education, discipline**. Hebrews 12:5–11 quotes Proverbs 3:11–12 and explains: “God is treating you as sons… he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.” Discipline “seems painful rather than pleasant,” but “later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.”

*Dikē* means **justice, or the penalty that justice requires** (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Jude 7). *Ekdikēsis* means **vindication, justice done**, often for the wronged: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Romans 12:19), and God will “give justice to his elect” (Luke 18:7). We leave vengeance to God because only he judges perfectly.

*Basanos* was first a **touchstone**, a dark stone used to test whether gold was real; the verb *basanizō* came to mean to test, then to torment. In Revelation 14:10 it describes torment with fire and sulphur, while in Matthew 14:24 the same verb describes a boat “beaten” by the waves. The word's roots lie in testing and proving.

sections.h: The Jewish context: sufferings of love
p: Jewish tradition took Proverbs 3:12 to heart. The Talmud speaks of *yissurin shel ahavah*, “sufferings of love” (Berakhot 5a): hardships that God allows not to destroy, but to draw a person closer. Lamentations says, “Though he cause grief, he will have compassion… for he does not afflict from his heart” (Lamentations 3:32–33). God takes no pleasure in pain.

Ezekiel puts it plainly: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Even in exile, the prophets always spoke of God's judgments as leading toward return and restoration (Hosea 11:8–9; Jeremiah 29:11–14).

sections.h: Common misunderstandings and living it out
p: A common Western picture treats God's punishment as mainly about satisfying offended honour, with pain as an end in itself. The Hebrew and Jewish lens does not deny that God judges or that sin has real and serious consequences. But it insists that God judges **as a father, a refiner and a rescuer**: to stop evil, defend the weak, and bring his children home.

This matters for how we live. When hardship comes, we can ask what God may be teaching, without assuming he is angry with us. When we correct our own children, students or friends, our goal should be their growth, not our satisfaction. And when we are wronged, we can leave justice in God's hands, trusting him to set things right (Romans 12:19–21).

chapters.title: Flesh and Body
chapters.subtitle: The Bible does not teach that the body is bad and the soul is good
chapters.trueMeaning: Frail human life, kinship, the whole person
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew, “flesh” (basar) means the body, human weakness, family ties and even all living creatures. It is not evil: God promises a “heart of flesh” and to pour out his Spirit “on all flesh”. Jews saw a person as one living whole, with a struggle between good and evil inclinations, not between a bad body and a good soul. When Paul contrasts “flesh” and “Spirit”, he means human life lived by its own strength versus life led by God's Spirit, not body against soul.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical “flesh” is frail human life, not an evil body; the body is good, and the real struggle is between living by our own power and living by God's Spirit.

sections.h: What we usually assume
p: Many Christians grow up with a quiet assumption: the **body** is the problem and the **soul** is what really matters. The body has desires that drag us down, while the soul is pure and will one day escape to heaven. When we read Paul's warnings about “the flesh”, it seems to confirm this picture.

That picture owes more to Greek philosophy than to the Bible. Thinkers like Plato taught that the body was a kind of prison for the soul. The Hebrew Scriptures, and the Jewish world of Jesus and Paul, saw things very differently. To read Paul well, we need to start with the Hebrew word *basar*.

sections.h: Basar: flesh, frailty and family
p: *Basar* literally means **flesh**, the soft tissue of the body, and by extension the **body** itself. But it is used in several wider ways. It means **kinship**: when Adam sees Eve he says, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), and Laban tells Jacob, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh” (Genesis 29:14). Husband and wife become “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

It means **human frailty**: “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6). God “remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again” (Psalm 78:39). It means **all people, or all living creatures**: “the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together” (Isaiah 40:5).

Flesh is weak, but it is not wicked. The psalmist asks, “What can flesh do to me?” (Psalm 56:4), and Jeremiah warns against the one who “makes flesh his strength” and turns from the LORD (Jeremiah 17:5). The problem is not having a body; it is **relying on mere human strength instead of God**.

sections.h: A heart of flesh and the Spirit on all flesh
p: Sometimes *basar* is even a word of hope. God promises, “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Here flesh means a heart that is soft, alive and able to respond, in contrast to a cold, hard stone.

Joel declares, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28; 3:1 in Hebrew Bibles), and Peter quotes this at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). God's Spirit does not avoid flesh; he fills it. A related word, *she'er*, also means **flesh or meat** and, like *basar*, a **close blood relative**: “None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives” (Leviticus 18:6, literally “the *she'er* of his flesh”).

sections.h: Nefesh: the whole living person
p: English Bibles often translate *nefesh* as “soul”, which makes us think of an invisible part living inside the body. But in Genesis 2:7, God forms the man from dust, breathes into him the breath of life, and “the man became a living *nefesh*”. He did not *receive* a soul; he *became* one. *Nefesh* is **the whole living person**, a breathing, hungry, feeling creature. Animals too are called living *nefesh* (Genesis 1:24).

So in Hebrew thinking a human being is **a unity**: body, breath, heart and mind together. There is no picture of a good soul trapped in an evil body. Jewish morning prayers even thank God for the body's workings in the blessing *Asher Yatzar*, praising the One who “formed the human being with wisdom”.

sections.h: The two inclinations: the Jewish picture of the struggle
p: If the body is not the enemy, where does the struggle with sin come from? Jewish tradition speaks of two inclinations in every person: the *yetzer hara*, the **evil inclination**, and the *yetzer hatov*, the **good inclination**. The idea is rooted in Genesis, where God sees that “every intention (*yetzer*) of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5; see 8:21).

The Mishnah reads “love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5) as “with both your inclinations, the good and the evil” (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). In other words, even our strong drives are to be directed toward loving God. A well-known midrash even says that without the evil inclination nobody would build a house, marry or have children. The drives are not evil in themselves; they must be **ruled and guided**.
> The battle is not body against soul. It is the whole person pulled between two directions: toward self or toward God.

sections.h: Sarx, sōma and the Word made flesh
p: In Greek, *sarx* is the Septuagint's usual word for *basar*. Its most famous use is shocking for anyone who thinks flesh is evil: “**The Word became flesh** and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). John even warns that denying “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” is a sign of false teaching (1 John 4:2). Paul can also use *sarx* neutrally: “the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God” (Galatians 2:20).

*Sōma* means **body**, and Paul speaks of it with great honour: “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19); “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). The body will not be thrown away but raised: “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44). *Kreas* simply means **meat** for eating (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 8:13), and *psychē*, like *nefesh*, usually means **life** or the living self (Mark 8:35).

sections.h: Paul's “flesh” and “Spirit”
p: When Paul sets “flesh” against “Spirit” (Romans 8:4–9; Galatians 5:16–24), he is using *sarx* in a special sense: **human life lived by its own power, cut off from God's Spirit**. Look at his list of “the works of the flesh”: alongside sexual sins he names “enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy” (Galatians 5:19–21). Most of these are not bodily sins at all; they are sins of pride and broken relationships.

This is why some translations that render *sarx* as “sinful nature” can mislead. They can suggest that the body, or some separate part of us, is evil by nature. Paul's picture is much closer to the Jewish two inclinations: the whole person can follow a self-centred direction or be led by God's Spirit. Even “nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18) describes human life on its own, without God's power, not the body as evil.

sections.h: Western misunderstandings and the Jewish lens
p: When the church moved into the Greek world, some groups, later called **Gnostics**, taught that matter and the body were evil and that salvation meant the soul escaping the body. The early church rejected this. It confessed that God created the material world good, that the Word truly became flesh, and that believers look forward to “the resurrection of the body”.

Yet the Greek picture has often crept back in, making Christians ashamed of their bodies or indifferent to physical needs. The Jewish lens corrects this: God made the body, Jesus took on a body, the Spirit lives in our bodies, and God will raise our bodies. The struggle is real, but it is about **which direction the whole person follows**.

sections.h: Living it out
p: If the body is a temple, we honour God by caring for it: rest, food, work and touch are not unspiritual. If “all flesh” is frail like grass, we can be gentle with human weakness, our own and others'. And if “flesh” in Paul means life lived by our own strength, then the answer is not hating our bodies but **walking by the Spirit** (Galatians 5:16), letting God's Spirit produce “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23) in our everyday, bodily lives.

words.note: Weak but not evil; “all flesh” means all people or all creatures.
Like basar, it can mean a close family member.
The man did not receive a nefesh; he became one.
God's Spirit is poured out on flesh, not kept away from it.
The pull toward selfishness and sin in every person.
The pull toward God and goodness; both are to serve love for God.

words.gloss: flesh; human life on its own
words.note: The Septuagint word for basar; in Paul often life apart from God's Spirit.
The body is good, a temple of the Spirit, and will be raised.
Flesh as food, with no moral meaning.
Usually the Greek for nefesh: the whole life, not a ghost inside.

left.label: Greek dualism
items: Body is bad, soul is good
Salvation is the soul escaping the body
Flesh means the physical body
Sin comes from bodily desire
The body is thrown away at death

right.label: Jewish lens
items: The whole person is one living unity
Salvation includes the resurrection of the body
Flesh means frail human life, often without God
Sin comes from a misdirected inclination of the heart
The body is God's temple and will be raised

children: Opposite of walking by the Spirit

verses.text: Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
And all flesh shall see it together… All flesh is grass.
I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?
Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.

keyPoints: Hebrew basar means body, kinship, human frailty and “all people”; it is weak but not evil.
God promises a “heart of flesh” and pours out his Spirit “on all flesh”.
Nefesh is the whole living person: the man “became a living nefesh” (Genesis 2:7).
Jewish teaching locates the struggle in two inclinations, not in body versus soul.
The Word became flesh, the body is a temple of the Spirit, and it will be raised.
In Paul, “flesh” often means human life by its own power; many “works of the flesh” are not bodily sins at all.
“Sinful nature” can mislead if it suggests the body is evil; the Gnostic view was rejected by the early church.
reflect: Have you ever felt that your body was “unspiritual”? How does John 1:14 challenge that?
Looking at Galatians 5:19–23, which “work of the flesh” and which “fruit of the Spirit” most need attention in your life?
How could you honour God this week with your body as well as your thoughts?

quiz.q: When Laban says to Jacob, “You are my bone and my flesh” (Genesis 29:14), what does “flesh” mean?
quiz.why: Basar often expresses kinship, as also in Genesis 2:23.

options: Received a soul into his body
Was given a body as a prison
quiz.why: He became a living nefesh: a whole living person, not a soul placed in a container.

quiz.q: Jewish tradition describes the inner struggle as a conflict between:
options: The yetzer hara and the yetzer hatov
quiz.why: Jewish teaching speaks of the evil and good inclinations, rooted in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21.

quiz.q: Which of these does Paul list among “the works of the flesh” in Galatians 5:19–21?
quiz.why: Many works of the flesh, such as jealousy, strife and divisions, are not bodily sins, showing that flesh means more than the body.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the body in 1 Corinthians 6:19?
options: It is a prison for the soul
It does not matter to God
It is a temple of the Holy Spirit
quiz.why: The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:44).

terms.def: Flesh or body; also kinship, human frailty and all living beings.
A living being; the whole person, often translated “soul”.
The evil inclination: the inner pull toward selfishness and sin.
The good inclination: the inner pull toward God and goodness.
Flesh; in Paul often human life lived by its own power apart from God's Spirit.
Body; good, a temple of the Spirit, and destined for resurrection.
